Photograph: Tamir Kalifa/Getty Images West Bank Israel indicts settler over death of Palestinian activist who worked on No Other Land Yinon Levy charged with manslaughter in first exception this decade to culture of impunity for Israelis who kill Palestinians in the occupied West Bank Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem Fri 7 Aug 2026 09.49 EDT First published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Prosecutors in Israel have indicted an extremist settler for shooting a Palestinian activist last July, the first attempt this decade to hold an Israeli responsible for killing a Palestinian in the occupied West Bank . Yinon Levy, who was under western sanctions, is charged with manslaughter over the death of Awdeh Hathaleen, an English teacher and peace activist. In his last moments, Hathaleen filmed the settler drawing his weapon and opening fire towards him. Hathaleen’s family said Levy should have been charged with first-degree murder over the well-documented attack in the village of Umm al-Khair. Reckless manslaughter carries a maximum prison sentence of 12 years, far less then murder. “This was not an accident,” said his cousin Tarek Hathaleen. “Yinon Levy must be held fully accountable for Awdeh’s killing.” The charges nevertheless represented a “significant development”, Hathaleen added, after years of near-total impunity for Israelis who attack Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. 0:53 Palestinian activist recorded moment he was killed by settler in West Bank – video My sweet friend Awdah Hathaleen was murdered by a West Bank settler. May his memory be a revolution | Emily Glick Read more Israeli settlers and soldiers have killed more than 1,500 Palestinians this decade, according to rights group B’tselem . Levy is the first person indicted over any of those deaths. Military prosecutors last brought charges over a 2019 shooting of a young man who stopped to help victims of a traffic accidentThe last time civilian prosecutors brought charges was in 2018 over the killing of a mother of eight, hit by a rock as she was driving. Settler violence and ethnic cleansing has surged in the occupied West Bank over the past three years, supported by far-right Israeli cabinet ministers who hold security, defence and finance portfolios. Levy’s indictment over one of the highest-profile killings in that period does not represent a policy shift for Israel, rights groups said. Hathaleen had worked on No Other Land , the Oscar-winning documentary about his community’s decades-long struggle against the Israeli state and settlers, to stay in their homes and lands in the south Hebron hills. “It’s important to see this killing as part of an ongoing and systematic situation in the West Bank,” said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Yesh Din, an Israeli rights and advocacy organisation. “I don’t think these charges are an indication of increased law enforcement or accountability. It is more likely due to the fact that [Awdeh Hathaleen] was a well-known activist and the case got a lot of media exposure and public critique. It’s more about an appearance of law enforcement, rather than actual law enforcement.” Levy, who was under sanctions for violence against Palestinians by the UK, EU, Canada and Australia at the time of the attack, was briefly detained last year but police released him after three days under house arrest. He spent the last year free and continued establishing illegal outposts in the occupied West Bank, said Yair Dvir, spokesperson for B’tselem. “The decision to indict Yinon Levy is the exception that proves the rule,” Dvir said. “The impunity Israel grants to soldiers and settlers who harm Palestinians is not a failure of the system – it is a central component of a policy designed to allow the violence to continue and escalate.” The culture of impunity spurred the former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the International Criminal Court to bring charges against “Jewish terrorists”, saying intervention was needed to halt the violence. Levy is also charged with armed trespassing and malicious property damage in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair. Before Hathaleen was shot, another settler drove a bulldozer through Palestinian land, destroying trees and property. When a resident approached and asked him to stop, the driver knocked the man down with the bulldozer blade. Even if the case goes to trial, any verdict could be many years away, and Israeli judges have a record of lenient treatment of Israelis who attack Palestinians. The Israeli soldier who shot 23-year-old Ahmad Manasrah dead in 2019 pleaded guilty to the equivalent of negligent homicide and was sentenced to three months community service for the killing. He has not been publicly named. Eight years after a 2018 attack that killed 47 year-old Aisha Rabi, an Israeli court ruled that a settler had thrown the stone that killed her. Judges did not hand down a conviction or sentence, instead ordering a review because the man, who was not named, was 16 at the time of the attack. No further details have been made public. Hathaleen’s family say they will continue to fight for Levy to face full trial. “Justice requires more than simply bringing a charge,” said Tarek Hathaleen. “Awdeh was not only my cousin. He was my childhood friend and someone very dear to me. His absence has left a pain that will never go away.” Sufian Taha contributed reporting Explore more on these topics West Bank Palestine Israel Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story How children in West Bank are being killed by Israel ‘without accountability’ Israeli police kill two young Palestinian boys and their parents in West Bank Israelis kill three in West Bank village as violence surges across occupied Palestine Senators demand investigation after ninth American killed by Israeli settlers or soldiers in West Bank Brother of No Other Land co-director injured as Israeli settlers again attack family home ‘A step in the wrong direction’: Israel’s West Bank plans prompt global backlash Palestine’s ambassador to UK hails embassy as ‘proof our identity cannot be denied’ Press Israel to release Marwan Barghouti, former world leaders urge Trump Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.express.co.uk/news/politics/.text: Home News Politics Nearly £4billion in loans and grants was issued (Image: Getty) Nearly one in five student loans have been handed to foreigners as fears grow the British taxpayer is now on the hook for billions. Research has found that nearly £4 billion in student loans and maintenance grants has been received by foreign students in the past twelve months. Students from the EU received the majority of that funding, with data showing foreign students are around 25 per cent less likely to repay loans. It would mean that the British taxpayer could be expected to pick up the tab for between £1.2 and £2.2 billion in unpaid fees each year. Read our Privacy Policy Student finance is normally restricted for international students, but under the terms of a post- Brexit deal, EU students or their relatives are exempt. Around one in every twenty of new first-time student loans made to international students are received by Romanian nationals, fuelling government concerns of fraud. Politics LIVE: Kemi Badenoch vows to end 'cash machine Britain' in crackdown on foreigners Under the terms of the post-Brexit agreement with Brussels people with settled status are entitled to claim student financial support. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT In the last year 36,000 people have successfully applied settled status, alongside 30,000 family members of those who already have it. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Data from the Student Loan Company shows that 239,000 foreign citizens have received loans, of which 195,000 have settled status under this scheme. Over the last decade the proportion of student loans handed to students not from the UK has jumped from 10.2 per cent to 19.3 per cent. Shadow Education Secretary, Laura Trott MP said: "British taxpayers shouldn't have to foot the bill for billions of pounds in loans to foreign students who may never pay them back. "It's not fair or sustainable. Labour needs to get a grip on the situation." Neil O'Brien, a Conservative MP, told the Daily Express there were "clear signs of abuse in the system" due to the amount of funding going to family members of those with settled status. Mr O'Brien said that the figures around the number of Romanians receiving funding was "mad" people would be "stunned that a fifth of all student loans are now going to people who are not British". A spokesman for the Department for Education said: "We have strict eligibility requirements for student loans - nobody who lives outside of the UK can apply for or receive a loan. "Anyone leaving the UK must continue to repay what they owe." Photograph: Oleksandr Gimanov/AFP/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Nine killed and dozens wounded in Russian strikes as Kyiv braces for harsh winter Zelenskyy says ‘Russia wants to kill the Ukrainian economy’ as Moscow steps up attacks on infrastructure. What we know on day 1,663 Guardian staff and agencies Sat 12 Sep 2026 21.22 EDT Last modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 21.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian airstrikes killed nine people, injured dozens and damaged buildings and infrastructure across Ukraine on Saturday, as Kyiv braces for a “very difficult” winter amid intensified attacks on the country. The civilian death toll has risen sharply in Ukraine over the past two ⁠months as Russia steps up attacks ⁠on power plants and other ​infrastructure. Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses in distant parts of Russia, and both sides have targeted each other’s shipping. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, writing on Telegram, said Russia had deployed nearly 500 drones against Ukrainian targets since ⁠early morning. “Basically, the Russians have expanded the war away from the front, where they have no success, into the economy, and their tactics are as basic as it gets: destroying every site that could help people cope with the conditions of war,” he wrote. “Russia ⁠wants to kill the Ukrainian economy and break our resistance.” The city council in Kramatorsk , one of Ukraine’s frontline “fortress cities” that Russia wants to capture, ​ said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people in three incidents over ‌a 90-minute period . Four people were injured. “These ‌are not military targets,” the council said. “They are ordinary civilian cars. People were going about their business.” View image in fullscreen A car that struck by a Russian drone in the frontline city of Kramatorsk. Photograph: Anatolii Stepanov/Reuters The governor of Ukraine’s Zhytomyr region, Vitaliy Bunechko, said ‌a Russian strike on a grocery store killed two people in the town of Zviahel, west of Kyiv. Bunechko said two petrol stations also came under attack. Earlier, Zelenskyy reported attacks on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih, his home town. The governor of Zaporizhzhia region, Ivan Fedorov, said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other localities . In Odesa region, governor Oleh Kiper said 37 people, including an infant, were injured in a ​series of overnight attacks, while two people were missing. Russia’s defence ministry said Russian forces have maintained their strikes on Ukrainian ports, hitting a cargo ship in Odesa that it said was carrying goods ⁠for military use. Ukrainian officials said the country was bracing for a brutal winter as intensified Russian attacks on infrastructure and key export industries compound a ⁠deepening budget crisis. The economy minister, ​Oleksandr Kravchenko, said damage to infrastructure and fixed assets from Russian airstrikes was estimated at close to $10bn this year, while the broader economic costs of the attacks and ⁠the de facto blockage of its ports had cut 1.5 percentage points of GDP. “We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day ⁠by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country,” he said. With fighting on the frontline largely stalled, Russia and Ukraine have increasingly ‌targeted logistics networks and other economic assets in an effort to undermine each other’s war effort . For more than two weeks, Russia has carried out near constant attacks on Kyiv using faster j et-powered drones , disrupting life, business and government operations. Moscow has also effectively blocked Ukraine’s Black Sea ports by intensifying its air attacks on the country’s southern regions. Ukraine’s ‌main exports – agricultural products and iron and steel – are shipped via these ports. In Moldova on Ukraine’s western border, authorities closed national airspace for nearly an hour after a drone was detected near the border. Seven border crossings were temporarily closed. Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami for talks on ending the war, in a media interview released Saturday, but the Kremlin immediately ruled it out. “It is impossible,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told AFP in New Delhi on Saturday, repeating Moscow’s demand that a meeting can only take place in the Russian capital. The gathering of world leaders takes place on 14-15 December and there has been no confirmation yet as to whether Putin would attend. Putin has repeatedly rejected offers for a face-to-face meeting with Zelenskyy. https://www.politico.eu/article/former-u.text: The United States cannot credibly defend freedom around the world while treating the survival of a democracy under attack as a bargaining chip. Russia’s war against Ukraine is not simply a territorial dispute. It is a test of whether democratic nations will defend the principles that sustain their freedom — or allow an authoritarian aggressor to destroy these principles through military force, terror and economic coercion. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine was unlawful. Its conduct has included attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and in March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova over alleged war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. All grave allegations that demand accountability. Advertisement Advertisement As Ukraine continues to fight for its survival, current U.S. policy raises a fundamental question: Does Washington understand what is at stake? If Moscow succeeds in subjugating Ukraine, other authoritarian leaders will also ask whether military conquest can succeed. Can U.S. commitments be trusted? Will democratic nations stand together when the price becomes politically inconvenient? Ukraine’s defense is not charity. It is a strategic investment in American and European security, Washington’s credibility and the deterrence of future conflicts. The U.S. emerged from World War II understanding that an international order based on sovereignty, freedom and rule of law serves its interests. And successive Republican and Democratic administrations recognized that unchecked authoritarian expansion threatens both American security and the independence of its allies. That understanding must guide U.S. policy toward Russia today. Diplomacy is essential. Negotiations to end the war should be pursued seriously. But peace cannot mean rewarding aggression, compelling Ukraine to surrender its sovereignty or giving Moscow time to rearm for another invasion. Advertisement Advertisement Appeasement does not necessarily prevent conflict. It can encourage aggression by convincing dictators the free world lacks the will to resist them. And a ceasefire without effective safeguards could become merely a pause before the next assault. A settlement that leaves Ukraine defenseless would postpone the conflict, not resolve it. Peace should be measured not by the speed with which an agreement is signed, but by whether it protects Ukraine’s independence and makes another war less likely. And economic pressure is among the most important nonmilitary instruments available to the U.S. in this process, as Russia’s ability to wage war depends substantially on energy revenues, access to international markets and networks that facilitate sanctions evasion. On Sept.18, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law. Then, on Oct. 16, he issued an executive order waiving specified sanctions, restrictions and duties authorized under the legislation, citing the national interest. This order raises a legitimate question about how Washington intends to use the economic leverage Congress provided. The measurable objectives these waivers are intended to achieve, why they serve American national security and what conditions would trigger their reconsideration need to be explained. The U.S. needs to enforce restrictions consistently, close avenues for evasion and impose consequences when countries or companies knowingly provide material assistance to Russia’s war effort in violation of applicable law. This does not require abandoning diplomacy. It requires a coherent policy in which economic relief advances clearly defined security objectives. Advertisement Advertisement If Washington weakens its own pressure without obtaining meaningful concessions, it risks surrendering leverage while leaving Russia’s aggression unresolved. Every source of revenue helping Moscow sustain its military campaign has consequences for Ukrainian civilians, who bear them in destroyed homes, shattered families and lost lives. U.S. policy should not make it easier for Russia to finance a war Washington says it wants to end. American history has a bipartisan tradition of leadership that combines the defense of freedom with strategic judgment. Harry Truman understood U.S. security depended on resisting authoritarian expansion. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, John F. Kennedy demonstrated that strength and diplomacy are not opposites. Ronald Reagan understood freedom must be defended against those who seek to suppress it. And George H. W. Bush knew sovereignty and alliances are essential to an international order where nations cannot redraw borders by force. Though from different eras, the leadership of these presidents reflected a common principle: American security is strengthened when the U.S. combines military strength, alliances, diplomacy and a commitment to the independence of free nations. A policy that pressures Ukraine more than Russia, offers Moscow economic relief without substantial concessions or asks Ukrainians to accept an insecure future is not a strategy for lasting peace. It risks rewarding aggression and inviting further conflict. Advertisement Advertisement And above all, Ukraine’s future should not be decided over the heads of Ukrainians. Democratic institutions can be attacked and dismantled far faster than they can be rebuilt. Ukraine’s struggle is therefore about more than one war. It is about whether the democratic world will remain a community of nations bound by common principles or become a collection of states left to negotiate individually with authoritarian regimes. History will not judge U.S. policy solely by the immediate cost of weapons, energy or sanctions. It will judge whether America stood by a nation fighting for survival, upheld the principles it asks others to respect and helped prevent future wars by demonstrating that aggression does not pay. Adrian Zuckerman is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2019-2021); Mark Gitenstein is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2009-2012) and to the EU (2022-2025); Ron Gidwitz is a former U.S. ambassador to Belgium (2018-2021) and acting U.S. ambassador to the EU (2020-2021); Jim Gilmore is a former U.S. ambassador to the OSCE (2019-2021); Kathleen Kavalec is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2023-2025); Jim Rosapepe is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (1998-2001).
